title: never blended as doctrine
hook: a Rig Veda line about one truth and many names, and what it does and doesn't say
tomorrow: four short sentences. what do they say we are?

segments.voice: Yesterday, never blended as doctrine stood in stone at Maghar: a samadhi and a mazar, two doors for one man. Today, the block's last day, and a line people love to quote.

A wedding toast, two families who pray differently, everyone a little nervous. Someone raises a glass: well, all religions are the same anyway. Everyone smiles. It's kind. But is it true? Someone may add an old Hindu line to back it up: the real is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. It comes from the Rig Veda. And in its own verse, it isn't talking about the world's religions at all.
screen: `ALL RELIGIONS ARE THE SAME?` → `THE REAL IS ONE.` → `NOT ABOUT RELIGIONS AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole verse, in paraphrase. They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni; it is the heavenly bird with lovely wings. The real is one; the wise speak of it in many ways, calling it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan. In its setting, the many names are Vedic gods. The poet is saying that behind the names his own tradition uses, there is one reality. Later readers widened it. Some Hindus take the line as a way to honor other paths too: the one truth may be named in many ways, by many peoples. Now notice what the line does, and what it doesn't. It makes room for respect. It doesn't say all teachings are the same teaching. Many names for the one isn't one creed for everyone. A Hindu who honors a Sufi saint can hold this verse and keep Hindu doctrine whole, while the shrine's Muslim keepers keep theirs. So what does it give you at that wedding? A way to be warm without pretending. We name what's holy in different ways is something a Hindu can say from inside this verse. We all believe the same thing is a bigger claim, and the verse doesn't make it. That closes this part of the path: Hinduism in the world, from Gandhi and King to shared saints, and now this.
screen: `INDRA, MITRA, VARUNA, AGNI.` · `LATER READERS WIDENED IT.` · `ROOM FOR RESPECT, NOT ONE CREED.` · then, large: `WARM, WITHOUT PRETENDING.`

segments.voice: Think of one table coming up where faiths mix: a dinner, a wedding, a holiday. Name a wish for it, to be kind and honest at once. Name what might get in the way, the urge to nod along or the urge to correct someone. Then choose one warm, true sentence you could say there, and say it to yourself once.
Never blended as doctrine. Respect for many names, without making them one creed: the way this history held its shared saints.
Something to keep: never blended as doctrine, many names for the one, and each house still its own. That closes this part of the path.

fork.setup: your uncle quotes 'the real is one; the wise speak of it in many ways' to prove every religion teaches the identical thing. what does the verse itself do?
options: it gives many Vedic names for one reality; it doesn't make all creeds one.
it lists the world's religions and declares them all equal.
it warns that only one name for the real is the correct one.
fork.reveal: In its hymn, the names are Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni and more. Later readers widened it into respect for other paths, not one creed.
